transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-04
Start: 16:00 PDT
Duration: ~58m
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Derek Huang (Redwood SE), James Ortega (Aurora CTO), Leah Kim (Lead ML Eng), Samir Patel (Infra), Nora (Product)

Auto-summary (auto gen): quick hosted api demo — streaming, params, retries, console tour.

---
[00:00] Maya: Hi everyone, thanks for joining — I'm Maya from Redwood, and with me is Derek from our systems team. How's everyone doing?
[00:07] James: Doing good, thanks. Busy week but excited for this.
[00:09] Leah: Yep, great to be here. We'll mostly be listening but Leah here will ask deep infra stuff.
[00:14] Maya: Perfect, we'll run an end-to-end quick demo, start with the API behavior for streaming responses, show param effects, and then go into retries and idempotency. We'll wrap with console metrics and next steps. Sound okay?
[00:25] James: Sounds good. Important for us: predictable latency under heavy loads, and cost per token.
[00:31] Maya: Got it, we'll call out tuning levers. Derek, quick callout before we jump in?
[00:35] Derek: Yeah, hi. I'll show the runtime behavior and talk about KV cache + batching briefly. Also preface that the hosted tier we're demoing has autoscaling and fallback models for graceful degradation.

[02:10] Maya: Ok I'll share my screen — console.redwood.ai (note: link demo instance). Deck and benchmark links in the chat: https://bit.ly/rwd-demo-deck and drive: https://drive.google.com/rwd-bench (these are placeholders in the transcript).
[02:30] Maya: Starting with a short chat example. Using the /v1/chat/completions endpoint (our Hosted API). I'm sending a system prompt and a user message. Derek, do you want to explain streaming frames?
[02:40] Derek: Sure. When you hit streaming, we open a chunked response and push delta tokens as they're generated. For short responses it's a steady stream, for long-form you see many small chunks. The important bits are: you can configure max_tokens, temperature, top_p and you can get partial tokens as they appear.
[03:08] Leah: Is there a difference in latency between streaming and sync?
[03:11] Derek: Streaming has slightly better perceived latency for users since you get early tokens as they generate; end-to-end completion latency is similar but perceived time-to-first-token is lower. Sync waits until chunk assembly is complete on our edge.

[05:23] Maya: Demo: baseline call with temp=0.2, max_tokens=150. (typing) Here we go — streaming response started at 230 ms, first token at ~120ms. Notice the console shows per-request timing and token count.
[05:42] James: 120ms first token — great. What's the backend model?
[05:46] Derek: For demo I'm using model var redwood-rlm-3b (a placeholder), which is quantized for cost efficiency. For production you can pin different variants — we show perf profiles in the catalog.

[07:10] Maya: Switching temperature to 0.9 — same prompt. You can see increased token variance and some creative output. This often affects cost because longer outputs mean more tokens.
[07:35] Leah: We tend to truncate outputs and post-process. Is there server-side support for stop sequences?
[07:39] Derek: Yes, stop sequences are fully supported. We also have content filters and policy controls if you need safety layers.

[09:02] Maya: Now let's show retry behavior. Simulating a transient error on our side — returning HTTP 5xx. Common pattern: client retries with exponential backoff and jitter, but you must consider idempotency or duplicate tokens.
[09:20] Derek: Right — for generation requests we recommend using idempotency keys for write-like operations (like data creation). For pure completion you can re-run with the same conversation context, but watch out for at-least-once semantics — duplicates are possible.
[09:38] Samir: For our service we need exactly-once for billing events. How do you handle that?
[09:42] Derek: For billing events you should use server-side event logs or transactional layers; we provide request-level metadata and audit logs. If you need strictly deduped responses, use idempotency keys and store the response server-side once it's first returned.

[12:00] Maya: Demo of backoff: client auto-retries with 500ms -> 1s -> 2s, and Redwood side returns a 503 for the first attempt, success on second. Console shows retry_count and latency distribution.
[12:24] James: Ok. What about request timeouts and partial streams? If client disconnects and reconnects, can we resume?
[12:32] Derek: We don't offer stream resume yet. If the client disconnects mid-generation, the KV cache may already have a prefix saved for subsequent requests, but the exact stream cannot be resumed. Best practice: checkpoint the prompt and use caching to reduce cost if you need to re-request.

[15:40] Leah: Can you explain the KV cache and prefix cache a bit more? We have long context windows and want to reuse prefixes across requests.
[15:48] Derek: Sure — our prefix/K-V cache stores recent key-values for transformer attention for hot prefixes. If your application reuses the same user history frequently, the runtime will reuse the KV cache which saves compute and lowers latency. Note some mispronunciations: in the transcript it might show as "K-V cash" or "K-V cache".
[16:12] Maya: Here's an example: we have conversation A that shares a large system prompt. When a new message arrives, using the same conversation_id will leverage the cached prefix so you don't recompute earlier tokens. This reduces per-token compute.

[19:05] James: How do batching and concurrency affect latency?
[19:09] Derek: Continuous batching groups requests on the GPU and raises throughput at the cost of per-request latency. For strict p95 latency you can configure low batch size and higher preemption to keep tails low. Redwood Dedicated gives you more control there.

[22:20] Maya: Quick Console tour: per-route token cost, p50/p95 latency, token breakdown by user vs system, and route-level controlled throttles. You can set alert thresholds on the console. (shows screen)
[22:45] Nora: Can we see retention / logs?
[22:49] Maya: Yes, audit logs and request traces are available in the private plane (note: says private plane but meant control plane). We'll attach the security pack.

[25:10] Leah: For prompt engineering, what's the suggested knob to reduce hallucinations?
[25:15] Derek: Lower temperature, set stop sequences, and provide structured prompts. Also consider post-reranking or a second-pass classifier. Our Optimize product can suggest quantization and model variants but also evaluation hooks to detect regressions.

[28:00] Maya: Cost control levers: choose smaller model variant, aggressive prefix caching, reduce max_tokens, and tune sampling params. For high throughput we recommend batching and Dedicated pools.
[28:27] James: If we go with hosted, what's the SLA?
[28:30] Maya: Hosted gives best time-to-value but lower contractual SLAs than Dedicated. We can offer enterprise SLA add-ons; we'll include details in the pricing doc.

[31:15] Derek: Demo: simulate a concurrency spike — console shows autoscale up, then fall back to cheaper model var if capacity constrained. The fallback is policy-based and can route to a lower-cost quantized variant.
[31:35] Samir: How do you ensure data isolation for logs if we have PHI?
[31:39] Maya: For PHI or regulated workloads we recommend Redwood Private (VPC/on-prem) with customer KMS support. Hosted can be configured w/ stricter retention and encryption, but for full isolation we use Private. We'll include the Private deployment checklist.

[34:50] Leah: A bit more on retries: if a stream fails after 80% complete, what's best practice? Do we resend the entire prompt?
[34:57] Derek: Two patterns: 1) Re-request from scratch with same messages and idempotency key, and dedupe on server; 2) If you can capture last-complete token offset, you can request a delta by conditioning on earlier cached KV state — but that requires persistent session support which is more of a Dedicated/Private feature today. For hosted, re-run with caching to cut compute.

[38:12] Maya: Let's run a short benchmark scenario — low temperature chat for customer support. I'll kick off 50 parallel streaming requests at small sizes. Watch the token throughput and 95th latency. (typing and running script)
[38:34] Derek: 50 parallel, average TTF (time-to-first-token) ~ 140ms, p95 ~ 680ms on this demo pool. Again, production numbers vary by model choice and region.

[41:50] James: If we need to limit cost spikes during a bad prompt, any recommendations?
[41:54] Derek: Add token caps (max_tokens), per-route hard quotas, and autoscaling throttle rules. You can also configure response truncation server-side and set cost alerts in the Console.

[45:22] Nora: Is there a way to get partial transcripts of streams in logs? We need them for compliance.
[45:29] Maya: Yes, request/response payloads can be retained in logs depending on retention policy and compliance package; for PHI we'd recommend Private deployment and minimal retention. We'll provide options in the security pack.

[48:00] Leah: For the pilot, we plan to run an internal benchmark with 1k requests/day, mixed short/long; we want to compare quantized vs FP model variants. Can Redwood provide a harness?
[48:09] Derek: Absolutely — I'll drop our benchmark harness and a sample load script. We'll also suggest prompt sets and evaluation metrics.

[51:20] Maya: Recap: 1) Demoed streaming and params, 2) covered retry/backoff and idempotency tradeoffs, 3) KV/prefix caching and batching implications, 4) Console metrics + security options.
[51:35] James: Good recap. Next: send security docs and sample harness. Let's target pilot kickoff next week.

[52:00] Maya: Action items: we'll share security pack and benchmark by Friday. Derek will send harness. Leah will provide prompt list.
[52:12] Samir: One quick question — region support for EU?
[52:15] Derek: Yes, we have EU regions and can route by customer policy. We'll confirm specific data residency options in writing.

[55:00] Maya: Anything else?
[55:04] James: No, that covers it. Thanks for the demo.
[55:09] Leah: Thanks everyone.
[55:12] Derek: Thanks, we'll follow up with links.
[55:20] Maya: Wrap up — ending recording.
